proof:
# A second deepest base pays an arbitrary regular circuit on a product interval This note proves individual Gamma_d efficiency in one genuine arithmetic regime: a complete one-dimensional integer interval with identical simplex fibers, whenever there is a second deepest base. The critical circuit may have arbitrary oblique normals and arbitrary normalized response weights. It is not assumed to be a canonical simplex circuit. This is a statement about one chosen actual critical circuit, not an assertion of universal stress allocation or unrestricted OC. ## 1. Definitions and precise theorem Let d>=1, let K be a full-dimensional d-simplex of volume V and centroid g, and let P={m,m+1,...,M} be a nonempty integer interval. Put S=P times K, with the measure which sums d-dimensional Lebesgue measure over its fibers. Let Q be its maximum raw halfspace depth, and let I subset P be the bases which contain points of depth Q. Fix an actual deepest point Y=(p,y) and a finite regular critical circuit H_j={a_j(z-p)+u_j dot (x-y)>=0}, mass(S intersect H_j)=Q, u_j !=0. (1) Here regular means that the cap-mass function is differentiable in the FULL hyperplane parameters (A,b), with the usual coarea first variation, not only in normals constrained to pass through the original source. A sufficient concrete condition is: every fiber trace is proper, strictly empty, or strictly full; more generally supporting traces with zero (d-1)-dimensional measure are allowed. Proper cuts of convex bodies have the usual first variation, and the condition excludes an unallocated positive supporting-facet jump. Assume there are positive numbers rho_j with sum_j rho_j u_j=0. (2) This is the continuous positive-circuit condition, so the H_j cover the whole plane z=p. Choose ANY theta_j>=0 with sum theta_j=1, in particular the response weights associated to this regular circuit, and put W(z,x)=sum_j theta_j 1_Hj(z,x). The boundary measure eta is the sum of H_(d-1) on the fiber boundaries, with n(x) the outward unit continuous normal where defined. A permissible potential is a nonnegative function Phi(n,z,x) convex in (z,x) for every fixed n; the explicit potential constructed below is continuous and has finite positive eta integral. **Theorem.** If I contains a base other than p, there exists such a potential with (integral Phi W d eta)/(integral Phi d eta) >= Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d. (3) The potential is supported, on the actual boundary bundle, on one of the two exposed endpoint fibers. Consequently (3) holds whenever I occupies every parity class occupied by P: if P has more than one point it occupies both parities, while the singleton case is immediate from its own fiber. ## 2. Exact strict-contact fact for regular critical caps For clarity, we recall the needed actual criticality argument. Suppose H through Y has nonzero continuous normal u and mass Q. Its own fiber cut is proper in the application below; thus its mixed coarea weight W_H is positive. At a depth-attaining cap through Y, differentiability of cap mass with respect to its normal gives sum_z integral_(K_z intersect boundary H) ((z,x)-Y) dH_(d-1)(x)=0. (4) The common factor 1/||u|| is immaterial. This is the full mixed section centroid identity, including the base coordinate, and follows because all sufficiently small normal perturbations through Y still contain Y and hence have mass at least Q. Every other deepest point Y' is strictly outside H. If it were in the interior, shifting the threshold slightly upward would retain Y' and remove positive volume from the proper own fiber, contradicting its depth Q. If it were on the boundary, differentiate caps through Y' at this same normal. By (4), their derivative in a perturbation delta A of the full normal is (W_H/||u||) delta A dot (Y-Y'). Taking delta A=Y'-Y gives a strictly negative derivative when Y'!=Y, again a contradiction. Finite positive coarea and regularity justify the first variation; the continuous normal remains nonzero in a neighborhood. No conclusion is inferred from section centroids without the actual minimum Q. For the simplex product, the proper-own-cut premise follows once y=g, which can be obtained without circular use of this fact as follows. A point y on boundary K cannot be a deepest point: a supporting through-y continuous halfspace captures zero d-volume from every identical fiber, while any interior point has positive raw depth (its own fiber has positive ordinary depth). Thus y is interior, so all u_j!=0 cuts through y are proper and the strict-contact argument applies from the outset. ## 3. All deepest points on a circuit's fiber are its centroid Raw depth, extended to the full ambient space, is quasiconcave. Indeed a closed halfspace containing a convex combination of points contains at least one of those points, so its mass is at least the minimum of their depths. Each permutation of the vertices of K is an affine bijection preserving uniform volume, S, and all ambient halfspaces. Averaging the finite orbit of any deepest point (q,x) therefore shows that (q,g) is also deepest and belongs to S. At the selected base p, suppose there were a different deepest point (p,y'). Section 2 makes it strictly outside every H_j. Multiplying these strict inequalities by rho_j and summing contradicts (2). Thus the fiber p has a unique deepest point, so y=g. This uses the chosen regular circuit and its positive balance; a single critical cap by itself would not prove uniqueness of the whole fiber. Choose q in I with q!=p. We have just shown that (q,g) is deepest, without needing any regularity premise at q. Section 2 applied to each H_j gives a_j(q-p)<0 for every j. (5) Thus all integer tilt coefficients have the same strict sign. ## 4. One exposed endpoint contains a through-centroid subcap in every row If q>p choose the left endpoint e=m. Equation (5) says a_j<0, hence a_j(e-p)>=0 for every j. If q

0 and the same conclusion holds. Thus each actual endpoint trace H_j restricted to {e} times K contains the parallel through-g halfspace trace K intersect {u_j dot (x-g)>=0}. (6) This is the decisive directional conclusion. The endpoint trace may be proper, full, or supporting. We do not identify its radial boundary integral with d times its offset cap volume; that equality would have a nonzero cut-plane flux. We use only the exact inclusion (6). ## 5. An admissible localized radial potential and its exact payment Let ell be an affine exposing function on the base interval, ell(e)=0, ell(z)<0 for every other z in P. Let R=max_(x in K)||x-g|| and choose a finite B with B(-ell(z))>=R for every z!=e. Define Phi(n,z,x)=[n dot (x-g)+B ell(z)]_+. (7) For each fixed n it is nonnegative and convex in the physical variables. At every actual boundary point of every nonendpoint fiber it vanishes. At the endpoint boundary, since g is interior to K, Phi(n(x),e,x)=n(x) dot (x-g)>=0. Consequently the divergence theorem gives its denominator exactly dV. For each through-g cap in (6), the cut-plane flux of the vector field x-g is zero. Its radial boundary integral is therefore exactly d times its cap volume. Closed-cap boundary intersections cause no loss: the cut passes through an interior point and is not a supporting facet of K. Ordinary Grünbaum for K at its centroid now gives integral_(boundary K intersect H_j at e) n dot (x-g) dH_(d-1) >= d |K intersect {u_j dot (x-g)>=0}| >= d Gamma_d V. (8) Multiply by theta_j and sum. The numerator is at least d Gamma_d V and the denominator is dV, proving (3). The calculation controls all oblique ambient caps in the actual circuit. It never replaces the selected point by a centroid outside its actual fiber. For d=1 the boundary measure is counting measure at the two interval endpoints; the same divergence identity is an endpoint identity and Gamma_1=1/2. For singleton P the source is the ordinary simplex centroid, and the same radial potential without localization pays Gamma_d. No boundary-potential assertion is made for d=0, where this normal-bundle measure is not defined. ## 6. Precisely what generalizes and what does not The argument works for any product K having a finite volume-preserving affine symmetry group whose orbit average is its centroid; ordinary Grünbaum, rather than simplex cap orientations, is used in (8). In arbitrary integer dimension the same proof of Sections 4--5 works if there is an EXPOSED vertex e of conv(P) with a_j dot (e-p)>=0 for every j, (9) after the sources have the same continuous centroid. This is a proved sufficient geometric condition, not an automatic consequence of occupied parity completion. The one-dimensional order supplies (9) from one other actual deepest base. Higher-dimensional base normals need not point in a common exposed-vertex direction, and no higher-dimensional implication is asserted here. Likewise varying fibers, nonregular critical circuits, and an arbitrary body without the stated centroid symmetry require additional arguments. ## 7. A different quantifier: selecting a paying circuit in every product rank There is a stronger selection result for product fibers which does not prove efficiency of an arbitrarily prescribed circuit. Let P be any finite integer base, in any integer dimension, and let S=P times K with the same simplex K. Suppose (p,g) is globally deepest and has at least one regular critical cap H={a dot (z-p)+u dot (x-g)>=0}, u!=0. For every affine vertex permutation of K, let G be its linear part in coordinates centered at g. Its image cap is H_G={a dot (z-p)+(G^(-T)u) dot (x-g)>=0}. (10) These remain actual globally critical and regular. Their integer coefficient a is the SAME in every row. The average of the maps G is zero, as is the average of their inverses, since the orbit average of every vector is zero. Hence sum_G G^(-T)u=0. Uniform positive coefficients therefore give a critical positive circuit; one may extract a positive minimal subcircuit if desired. No assertion about arbitrary old response weights or arbitrary old cap lists is used. Choose an exposed vertex e of conv(P) maximizing a dot z. Such a vertex exists, including a=0. It satisfies a dot(e-p)>=0. Every cap (10) at e therefore contains its parallel through-g cap. Apply the localized radial potential from Section 5, now with any affine function exposing this single e. It pays Gamma_d for EVERY normalized weight choice on this new cap list. The point (p,g) is an actual mixed point, and the selection did not change its depth or introduce extra fibers. If one starts with a regular critical circuit at a deepest point (p,y), the argument of Section 3 applies in any integer rank and gives y=g, so the same selection applies. The conclusion also extends to a common fiber having a finite volume-preserving affine symmetry group with zero average linear representation and centroid g. This selection result is consistent with the exact R4 counterexample: that counterexample disproves the universal claim for EVERY prescribed critical profile. Its canonical cap list has different integer tilts. Starting from just one of its caps and taking only continuous vertex permutations keeps one common integer tilt; an exposed base then pays the new circuit. The distinction matters whenever a proof is free to select one circuit per fixed witness. It gives no analogous selection theorem for genuinely different fibers, where the continuous permutations need not preserve the mixed family.
